claim: FBXL10, RNF68, and RNF2 exist in a trimeric complex.
source: We confirmed that the three proteins exist in a trimeric complex by performing sequential co-precipitation experiments in which we found that FBXL10-interacting RNF2 also interacted with RNF68 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A demonstrating physical interaction between the three proteins.

claim: Endogenous FBXL10, RNF68, and RNF2 are recruited to sites of DNA damage and co-localize with γH2A.X.
source: We found that endogenous FBXL10, RNF68, and RNF2 recruited to sites of DNA damage and co-localized with γH2A.X (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B after laser micro-irradiation.

claim: There is a significant increase in cross-correlation signal between FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 and XRCC5 upon NCS treatment.
source: We observed a significant increase in cross-correlation signal between FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 and XRCC5, upon NCS treatment (Figure 1B), showing an enrichment of the FRRUC at sites of DNA damage in agreement with the results obtained with laser micro-irradiation.
evidence: Supported by dSTORM super-resolution imaging and cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: XRCC5 is recruited very rapidly to DSBs before the choice of homologous recombination repair (HRR) versus non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) is made by the cell.
source: XRCC5 is recruited very rapidly before the choice of homologous recombination repair ﻿(HHR)﻿ v. non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) is made by the cell.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about XRCC5 recruitment kinetics and its role in DNA repair pathway choice.

claim: XRCC5 associates with chromatin in both undamaged and damaged cells.
source: Because it associates with chromatin in both undamaged and damaged cells, XRCC5 is an ideal marker to evaluate cross-correlation changes with other DNA-binding proteins in response to DNA damage (Britton et al., 2013; Reid et al., 2015; Teixeira-Silva et al., 2017; Walker et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Britton et al., 2013; Reid et al., 2015; Teixeira-Silva et al., 2017; Walker et al., 2001).

claim: GFP-FBXL10, mCherry-RNF68, and GFP-tagged RNF2 are recruited within seconds to laser-induced DNA damage spots.
source: When we tested the recruitment to laser-induced 'DNA damage spots' (Young et al., 2015), we found that GFP-FBXL10, mCherry-RNF68, and GFP-tagged RNF2 were recruited within seconds to these spots (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating rapid recruitment kinetics.

claim: The peak of recruitment of FBXL10, RNF68, and RNF2 to DNA damage sites is reached by approximately within one minute post-irradiation.
source: The peak of recruitment was reached by approximately within one minute post-irradiation, after which the signal progressively decreased (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by time-course live cell imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: RNF2 remains at DNA lesions longer than FBXL10 and RNF68.
source: We noticed that whereas the kinetics of disappearance of FBXL10 and RNF68 were comparable, RNF2 remained at DNA lesions for longer, likely because of its presence in both cPRC1s and ncPRC1s.
evidence: Based on observed kinetics data and inference about RNF2's participation in multiple complexes.

claim: FBXL11 does not recruit to laser-induced DNA damage sites.
source: Notably, no recruitment of FBXL11 (also known as FBL11, JHDM1A, and KDM2A), a close paralog of FBXL10 that does not bind RNF2 and RNF68 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), was observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that FBXL10 plays a specific role in the DDR.
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and binding data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Inhibition of PARP with Olaparib completely abolishes the recruitment of the FRRUC to sites of DNA damage.
source: Only the inhibition of PARP [Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase] with Olaparib completely abolished the recruitment of the FRRUC to sites of DNA damage (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,D).
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,D with PARP inhibitor treatment.

claim: Inhibition of ATM, ATR, or DNA-PK does not abolish recruitment of the FRRUC to DNA damage sites.
source: To test whether the recruitment of the FRRUC to sites of DNA damage depends on known DNA damage signaling enzymes, we evaluated the recruitment of the three subunits upon treatment of cells with small molecules to inhibit ATM (with KU60018), ATR (with AZ20), DNA-PK (with NU7441), and PARP (with Olaparib)(Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,D). Only the inhibition of PARP [Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase] with Olaparib completely abolished the recruitment of the FRRUC to sites of DNA damage (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,D).
evidence: Inferred from the statement that only PARP inhibition abolished recruitment, implying other kinase inhibitors did not.

claim: PARP inhibition with Olaparib abolishes recruitment of endogenous FBXL10, RNF68, and RNF2 to DNA damage sites.
source: Importantly, inhibition of PARP with Olaparib also abolished the recruitment of endogenous proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PARP1 catalyzes the production of long chains of branched poly(ADP)ribose on target proteins during the DNA damage response.
source: PARP1 is a critical sensor of DNA damage lesions, catalyzing the production of long chains of branched poly(ADP)ribose on target proteins during the DNA damage response (DDR) (Li and Yu, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li and Yu, 2015.

claim: PARylation occurs on substrates such as histones, certain DNA repair factors, and PARP1 itself.
source: PARylation is one of the earliest post-translational modifications in response to DNA lesions, occurring on substrates such as histones, certain DNA repair factors, and PARP1 itself (Rouleau et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rouleau et al., 2010.

claim: TIMELESS forms a near stoichiometric complex with PARP1.
source: We, and others, have shown that TIMELESS forms a near stoichiometric complex with PARP1 (Xie et al., 2015; Young et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Xie et al., 2015 and Young et al., 2015.

claim: Depletion of either PARP1 or TIMELESS abolishes the recruitment of FBXL10, RNF68, and RNF2 to sites of DNA damage.
source: Therefore, we monitored the recruitment of the FRRUC to sites of DNA damage after silencing either PARP1 or TIMELESS, finding that the recruitment of all three proteins was abolished after depletion of either PARP1 or TIMELESS (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A with siRNA knockdown.

claim: The recruitment of XRCC1 and Ligase 3 is affected by PARP1 silencing.
source: In contrast, the recruitment of other DNA repair factors, such as XRCC1 and Ligase 3, which are affected by PARP1 silencing (Campalans et al., 2013; Godon et al., 2008; Mortusewicz et al., 2006; Okano et al., 2003), were not affected by TIMELESS depletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by citations to Campalans et al., 2013; Godon et al., 2008; Mortusewicz et al., 2006; Okano et al., 2003.

claim: The recruitment of XRCC1 and Ligase 3 is not affected by TIMELESS depletion.
source: In contrast, the recruitment of other DNA repair factors, such as XRCC1 and Ligase 3, which are affected by PARP1 silencing (Campalans et al., 2013; Godon et al., 2008; Mortusewicz et al., 2006; Okano et al., 2003), were not affected by TIMELESS depletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The PARP1-TIMELESS complex promotes the rapid recruitment of the FRRUC to sites of DNA damage.
source: Collectively, our results demonstrate that the PARP1-TIMELESS complex promotes the rapid recruitment of the FRRUC to sites of DNA damage, suggesting an early role for this ubiquitin ligase complex in the response to DNA damage.
evidence: Based on integration of multiple experimental results showing PARP1 and TIMELESS dependence.

claim: RNF51-RNF2 and RNF110-RNF2 are components of two distinct cPRC1s that recruit to DNA lesions and mono-ubiquitylate H2A.
source: Since two dimeric ubiquitin ligases (RNF51-RNF2 and RNF110-RNF2), which are component of two distinct cPRC1s, have been shown to recruit to DNA lesions and mono-ubiquitylate H2A (Bergink et al., 2006; Ginjala et al., 2011; Gracheva et al., 2016; Ismail et al., 2010; Pan et al., 2011), we asked whether the recruitment of the FRRUC depends on the recruitment of these cPRC1 components.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bergink et al., 2006; Ginjala et al., 2011; Gracheva et al., 2016; Ismail et al., 2010; Pan et al., 2011.

claim: The recruitment of FBXL10 and RNF68 is not affected by the depletion of either RNF51 or RNF110.
source: We found that the recruitment of FBXL10 and RNF68 was not affected by the depletion of either RNF51 (also called BMI1 or PCGF4) or RNF110 (also called MEL18 or PCGF2) (Figure 2A-and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The recruitment of RNF2 is partially inhibited by the depletion of either RNF51, RNF110, or RNF68.
source: The recruitment of RNF2 was partially inhibited by the depletion of either RNF51, RNF110, or RNF68, likely because of its presence in both cPRC1s and ncPRC1s.
evidence: Based on observed recruitment data and inference about RNF2's participation in multiple complexes.

claim: GFP-tagged RNF51 and RNF110 recruit to laser induced DNA damage sites with peak recruitment around ~75 s post-irradiation.
source: Both GFP-tagged RNF51 and RNF110 recruited to laser induced DNA damage sites which peeks approximately around ~75 s post-irradiation and they remain at DNA lesions longer than FBXL10 and RNF68.
evidence: Based on live cell imaging kinetics data.

claim: The recruitment of RNF51 and RNF110 depends on PARP1 and TIMELESS presence as well as PARP1 activity.
source: We found that the recruitment of RNF51 and RNF110 depends on PARP1 and TIMELESS presence as well as PARP1 activity (Figure 2B–C-and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 2B-C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Four amino acids at position 251–254 of human RNF68 (QYSV) are essential for stable binding with FBXL10.
source: We found that four amino acids at position 251–254 of human RNF68 (QYSV) are essential for a stable binding with FBXL10 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data with truncation mutants shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutation of tyrosine 252 to aspartic acid in RNF68 significantly reduces RNF68's binding to FBXL10 without affecting its interaction with RNF2.
source: Further refinement of the interaction surface between RNF68 and FBXL10 indicated that mutation of tyrosine 252 to aspartic acid [generating RNF68(Y252D)] significantly reduced RNF68's binding to FBXL10 without affecting its interaction with RNF2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutation of Y252 to alanine in RNF68 has no effect on RNF68's interaction with FBXL10.
source: In contrast, mutation of Y252 to alanine [generating RNF68(Y252A)] had no effect on RNF68's interaction with FBXL10.
evidence: Based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Deletion of the RING domain of RNF68 completely abrogates its binding to RNF2 while leaving its interaction with FBXL10 intact.
source: Deletion of the RING domain of RNF68 [creating RNF68(ΔRING)] completely abrogated its binding to RNF2, while leaving its interaction with FBXL10 intact (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that RNF2 is not required for the interaction between FBXL10 and RNF68, in agreement with the crystal structure of the minimal version of ncPRC1.1 (Wong et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and citation to Wong et al., 2016.

claim: Wild-type RNF68, but not RNF68 inactive mutants, partially prevents the inhibition of RNF51's and RNF110's recruitment due to RNF68 silencing.
source: We found that wild-type RNF68, but not RNF68 inactive mutants, partially prevented the inhibition of RNF51's and RNF110's recruitment due to RNF68 silencing (Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 2B-C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RNF68's interaction with both RNF2 and FBXL10 is necessary for the proper recruitment of RNF51 and RNF110.
source: These results demonstrate that RNF68's interaction with both RNF2 and FBXL10, which is required form an active FRRUC, is necessary for the proper recruitment of RNF51 and RNF110.
evidence: Based on integration of mutant rescue experiments showing both interactions are required.

claim: An active FRRUC is necessary for the proper recruitment of cPRC1 complexes in response to DNA damage.
source: Thus, it appears that an active FRRUC is necessary for the proper recruitment of cPRC1 complexes, similarly to what was previously shown for transcriptional repression in unperturbed cells.
evidence: Based on experimental data and comparison to known function in transcriptional regulation.

claim: Knocking down FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 results in a significant reduction of H2AK119Ub1 staining on laser damage tracks.
source: Knocking down either FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) resulted in a significant reduction of H2AK119Ub1 staining on the laser damage tracks compared to control samples (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Silencing PARP1 or TIMELESS results in a decrease in H2AK119Ub1 levels at sites of DNA damage.
source: Likewise, silencing PARP1 or TIMELESS, which are required for proper localization of the complex, or inhibition of PARP, resulted in a decrease in H2AK119Ub1 levels at sites of DNA damage (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Wild-type RNF68, but not RNF68(ΔRING) or RNF68(Y252D), can rescue the defects in H2AK119Ub1 levels at DNA damage sites upon RNF68 depletion.
source: We found that, in contrast to the siRNA-resistant wild type RNF68, neither the siRNA-resistant RNF68(ΔRING) nor the siRNA-resistant RNF68(Y252D) could rescue the defects in H2AK119Ub1 levels at DNA damage sites (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Levels of H2AK119Ub1 are induced ~4.2 kbp from DSB sites and to a slightly lesser extent ~10.2 kbp from DSB sites.
source: Using qChIP with specific primers for a region downstream to the DSBs, we observed that levels of H2AK119Ub1 were induced ~4.2 kbp from the break sites, and to a slightly lesser extent ~10.2 kbp, from the DSB sites (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by qChIP data shown in Figure 3C using the FokI reporter system.

claim: Depletion of FBXL10, RNF2, or RNF68 strongly reduces the amount of H2AK119Ub1 detected at sites of DSBs.
source: Depletion of FBXL10, RNF2, or RNF68 (but not of XRCC6, used as a negative control) strongly reduced the amount of H2AK119Ub1 detected at the sites of DSBs (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), indicating that these proteins significantly contribute to the mono-ubiquitylation of H2A at K119.
evidence: Supported by qChIP data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The H2AK119Ub1 modification has been strongly associated with transcriptional silencing at DSBs.
source: The H2AK119Ub1 modification has been strongly associated with transcriptional silencing at DSBs (Kakarougkas et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2016, 2010; Ui et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kakarougkas et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2016, 2010; Ui et al., 2015.

claim: The production of nascent RNA transcript is almost completely abolished in control cells upon activation of the FokI nuclease.
source: The production of nascent RNA transcript was almost completely abolished in control cells upon the activation of the FokI nuclease (Figure 4B), indicative of transcriptional repression at sites of DNA damage.
evidence: Supported by YFP-MS2 reporter assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ATM inhibition significantly restores transcription near DSB sites.
source: As previously reported (Shanbhag et al., 2010), ATM inhibition significantly restored transcription near the DSB sites.
evidence: Supported by citation to Shanbhag et al., 2010 and experimental data.

claim: Depletion or mislocalization of the FRRUC significantly de-represses transcription near sites of DSB.
source: Depletion or mislocalization of the FRRUC (the latter accomplished through inhibition of PARP or depletion of either PARP1 or TIMELESS) also significantly de-repressed transcription near sites of DSB (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by YFP-MS2 reporter assay data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Silencing of FBXL10, RNF68, RNF2, PARP1, or TIMELESS does not have a negative effect on FokI nuclease levels.
source: Silencing of FBXL10, RNF68, RNF2, PARP1, or TIMELESS did not have a negative effect on FokI nuclease levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Nascent RNA production is significantly less reduced at sites of DNA damage in cells in which the FRRUC is depleted or mislocalized.
source: Nascent RNA transcript production at DNA damage stripes was significantly reduced in control cells (Figure 4D). By contrast, nascent RNA production was significantly less reduced at sites of DNA damage in cells in which the FRRUC was either depleted by siRNA or mislocalized by inhibiting PARP1 or by depleting either PARP1 or TIMELESS (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by 5-EU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Phosphorylation of RNAPII on Ser2 is impaired at break sites in control cells but significantly less impaired in cells depleted of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2, or in which the complex is mislocalized.
source: As expected, phosphorylation of RNAPII on Ser2 was impaired at break sites in control cells but was significantly less impaired in cells in which FBXL10, RNF68 or RNF2 were depleted, or in which the complex was mislocalized by either inhibiting PARP or depleting PARP1 or TIMELESS (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by RNAPII Ser2 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The FRRUC is required for transcriptional silencing after DNA damage.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that the FRRUC is required for transcriptional silencing after DNA damage.
evidence: Based on integration of multiple transcription assay results.

claim: The silencing of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 results in a significant reduction in the number of cells having DNA damage-induced foci containing RAD51.
source: The silencing of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 resulted in a significant reduction in the number of cells having DNA damage-induced foci containing the RAD51 recombinase (Figure 5A–B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence foci counting data shown in Figure 5A-B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Depletion of the FRRUC does not affect overall RAD51 protein levels.
source: At the same time, depletion of the FRRUC did not affect overall RAD51 protein levels as assessed by immunoblotting in both MIA-PaCa-2 and U-2OS cells (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), indicating that the complex acts by reducing the recruitment of RAD51 to chromatin rather than altering RAD51 levels.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Fewer cells contain BRCA1 foci after knockdown of FBXL10 or RNF68, and to a lesser extent after depletion of RNF2.
source: In addition, fewer cells contained BRCA1 foci after knockdown of FBXL10 or RNF68, and to a lesser extent after depletion of RNF2 (Figure 5A–B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence foci counting data shown in Figure 5A-B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Silencing FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 results in a significant reduction in the number of cells containing foci marked with phosphorylated RPA2 (pRPA2-S33).
source: Silencing FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 also resulted in a significant reduction in the number of cells containing foci marked with phosphorylated RPA2 (pRPA2-S33), a signal associated with stretches of ssDNA (Vassin et al., 2009) (Figure 5A–B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence foci counting data shown in Figure 5A-B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B, and citation to Vassin et al., 2009.

claim: Phosphorylation of RPA2 on Ser4, Ser8, and Ser33 is reduced upon depletion of the FRRUC.
source: This result was confirmed using immunoblotting, which showed that phosphorylation of RPA2 on Ser4, Ser8, and Ser33 was reduced (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Levels of phosphorylated CHK1 (Ser317) are lower after depletion of the FRRUC.
source: Similarly, levels of phosphorylated CHK1 (Ser317) (which indicates CHK1 activation upon genotoxic stress) were lower after depletion of the FRRUC.
evidence: Based on immunoblotting data.

claim: The levels of γH2A.X are similar in FRRUC-silenced cells compared to control cells.
source: In contrast, the levels of γH2A.X were similar in silenced cells (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), indicating that the amount of DNA damage induction was similar in all conditions.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Depletion of the FRRUC results in a significant reduction in the number of cells displaying ubiquitin-positive foci.
source: We observed that the depletion of the FRRUC resulted in a significant reduction in the number of cells displaying ubiquitin-positive foci (Figure 5A–B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by FK2 antibody immunofluorescence foci counting data shown in Figure 5A-B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The percentage of cells containing γH2A.X or MDC1 foci does not change by depleting FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2.
source: The percentage of cells containing γH2A.X or MDC1 foci (MDC1 recruitment is one of the most upstream events in the DDR) did not change by depleting either FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence foci counting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: Stable expression of siRNA-resistant wild type RNF68 significantly rescues the number of RAD51, BRCA1, pRPA32-S33, and FK2 foci in RNF68 depleted cells.
source: The stable expression of an siRNA-resistant wild type RNF68 construct in RNF68 depleted cells was able to significantly rescue the number of RAD51, BRCA1, pRPA32-S33, and FK2 foci (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Neither siRNA-resistant RNF68(ΔRING) nor siRNA-resistant RNF68(Y252D) can rescue the defects in the DDR due to RNF68 depletion.
source: In contrast, neither the siRNA-resistant RNF68(ΔRING) nor the siRNA-resistant RNF68(Y252D) could rescue the defects in the DDR due to RNF68 depletion (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The interaction of RNF68 with both FBXL10 and RNF2 is necessary for the assembly of DNA repair foci.
source: These results demonstrate that the interaction of RNF68 with both FBXL10 and RNF2, which is necessary to form an active FRRUC, is also necessary for the assembly of DNA repair foci.
evidence: Based on integration of mutant rescue experiments.

claim: Disruption of the FRRUC negatively affects the recruitment of HRR factors to sites of DNA damage and the downstream DDR.
source: Collectively, our results demonstrate that disruption of the FRRUC negatively affects the recruitment of HRR factors to sites of DNA damage and the downstream DDR.
evidence: Based on integration of multiple DDR marker experiments.

claim: DR-GFP cells depleted of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 exhibit significantly diminished abilities to perform HRR.
source: DR-GFP cells depleted of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 exhibited significantly diminished abilities to perform HRR (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by DR-GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Mislocalization of the FRRUC by silencing PARP1 or TIMELESS results in reduced HRR capacity.
source: Moreover, the mislocalization of the complex by silencing of PARP1 or TIMELESS also resulted in reduced HRR capacity (Figure 5E), in agreement with previous reports (Xie et al., 2015; Young et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by DR-GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 5E and citations to Xie et al., 2015; Young et al., 2015.

claim: Depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, RNF2, PARP1 or TIMELESS does not have any appreciable impact on cell cycle distribution.
source: Importantly, depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, RNF2, PARP1 or TIMELESS did not have any appreciable impact on cell cycle distribution, as shown by BrdU-PI staining (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), ensuring that the effects on the HHR pathway are not secondary to cell cycle differences.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: No significant reduction in DNA repair mediated by NHEJ is observed upon depletion of RNF68 or RNF2.
source: No significant reduction in DNA repair mediated by NHEJ was observed upon depletion of RNF68 or RNF2, as assessed by employing a cNHEJ assay based on the EJ5-GFP reporter U-2OS cell line (Bennardo et al., 2008) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by EJ5-GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and citation to Bennardo et al., 2008.

claim: Depletion of FBXL10 results in a reduction in NHEJ.
source: Depletion of FBXL10 resulted in a reduction in NHEJ (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E), in agreement with the reduction in 53BP1 foci (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–C), again, suggesting that FBXL10 may play a role in NHEJ independently of RNF68 and RNF2.
evidence: Supported by EJ5-GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and 53BP1 foci data.

claim: The reduction in the DDR and HRR in cells depleted of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 correlates with an increased sensitivity to DNA damage.
source: Finally, the reduction in the DDR and HRR in cells depleted of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2, correlated with an increased sensitivity to DNA damage as shown by the survival curves of cells treated with increasing concentrations of NCS (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2F.

claim: H2A levels are significantly reduced at FokI nuclease-induced DNA damage sites.
source: We observed that, despite the relative increase in H2AK119Ub1 levels (Figure 3A–C), H2A levels were significantly reduced at the FokI nuclease-induced DNA damage sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), in agreement with previous reports (Batenburg et al., 2017; Berkovich et al., 2007; Strickfaden et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by qChIP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and citations to Batenburg et al., 2017; Berkovich et al., 2007; Strickfaden et al., 2016.

claim: The reduction of H2A at DNA damage sites is inhibited by depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2.
source: Importantly, this reduction was inhibited by the depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2, suggesting that the FRRUC is involved in the eviction of H2A near DNA damage sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by qChIP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H2A.Z has been shown to be rapidly incorporated into sites of DNA damage and has been implicated in making the chromatin less compact to facilitate DNA repair.
source: H2A.Z has been shown to be rapidly incorporated into sites of DNA damage and has been implicated in making the chromatin less compact to facilitate DNA repair (Alatwi and Downs, 2015; Gursoy-Yuzugullu et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alatwi and Downs, 2015; Gursoy-Yuzugullu et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2012.

claim: The ratio of H2A.Z over H2A is increased ~4.2 and ~10.2 kbp from DSBs 1 hour after FokI induction.
source: To test whether the reduction in H2A is accompanied by a corresponding increase in the variant H2A.Z histone, we monitored the recruitment of H2A.Z to FokI-induced DSBs by qChIP 1 hr after induction, finding that the ratio of H2A.Z over H2A was increased ~4.2 and ~10.2 kbp from the DSB (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by qChIP data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The increase in H2A.Z/H2A ratio at DSBs is abolished after depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2.
source: This increase was abolished after depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2, demonstrating that the FRRUC is necessary for the enrichment of H2A.Z into sites of DNA damage (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by qChIP data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Four hours after induction of FokI, the relative enrichment of H2A.Z over H2A is still detectable, although to a lesser extent.
source: Four hours after induction of FokI, the relative enrichment of H2A.Z over H2A was still detectable, although to a lesser extent (Figure 6B), in agreement with previous reports of transient incorporation of H2A.Z at DNA lesions (Gursoy-Yuzugullu et al., 2015; Kalocsay et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by qChIP data shown in Figure 6B and citations to Gursoy-Yuzugullu et al., 2015; Kalocsay et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2012.

claim: H2A.Z is enriched at DNA damage sites as shown by dSTORM imaging.
source: First, we confirmed that H2A.Z was enriched at DNA damage sites (Figure 6C), similarly to FBXL10, RNF68, and RNF2 (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by dSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The magnitude of correlation between H2A.Z and γH2A.X diminishes upon depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2.
source: Importantly, analysis of H2A.Z and γH2A.X in cells treated with NCS showed that the magnitude of their correlation diminished upon depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), a further indication that the FRRUC is required for H2A.Z localization to sites of DNA damage.
evidence: Supported by dSTORM cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Mislocalization of the FRRUC through inhibition of PARP or depletion of PARP1 or TIMELESS results in failure to properly localize H2A.Z at sites of DNA damage.
source: Accordingly, mislocalization of the FRRUC (through inhibition of PARP or depletion of PARP1 or TIMELESS) also resulted in the failure to properly localize H2A.Z at sites of DNA damage (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by dSTORM cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Stable expression of siRNA-insensitive wild-type RNF68 rescues the effect of RNF68 depletion on H2A.Z recruitment.
source: To control for possible off-target effects of the siRNA, we stably expressed an siRNA-insensitive RNF68 construct and found that it was able to rescue the effect of RNF68 depletion (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Stable expression of siRNA resistant RNF68(Y252D) or RNF68(ΔRING) is unable to complement the defect in H2A.Z recruitment in RNF68-depleted cells.
source: In contrast, stable expression of either an siRNA resistant RNF68(Y252D) or an siRNA resistant RNF68(ΔRING) was unable to complement the defect in H2A.Z recruitment seen in RNF68-depleted cells (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that the ability to bind both FBXL10 and RNF2 to establish an active FRRUC is important in this process.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The FRRUC is required for proper H2A.Z recruitment to sites of DNA damage.
source: Combined, these measurements establish that the FRRUC is required for proper H2A.Z recruitment to sites of DNA damage.
evidence: Based on integration of multiple H2A.Z localization experiments.

claim: In unperturbed human cells, the incorporation of H2A.Z-H2B dimers into nucleosomes relies on the SCRAP and P400 chromatin remodeler complexes.
source: In unperturbed human cells, the incorporation of H2A.Z-H2B dimers into nucleosomes relies on the SCRAP and P400 chromatin remodeler complexes (Choi et al., 2009; Gévry et al., 2007; Ruhl et al., 2006), with the P400 complex being involved in the incorporation of H2A.Z also upon DSBs (Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Choi et al., 2009; Gévry et al., 2007; Ruhl et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2012.

claim: TIP48 and TIP49 accumulate on γH2A.X tracks after laser micro-irradiation.
source: We used laser micro-irradiation to induce local DNA damage in human U-2OS cells, which was visualized by γH2A.X staining, and detected an accumulation of TIP48 and TIP49 on the γH2A.X tracks.
evidence: Based on immunofluorescence microscopy observations.

claim: Depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 does not affect the recruitment of TIP48 and TIP49 to DNA damage sites.
source: We found that depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 did not affect the recruitment of TIP48 and TIP49 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G-H.

claim: Wild-type H2A and H2A(K119/120R) are equally incorporated in chromatin.
source: These two constructs were equally incorporated in the chromatin, as detected by ChIP, and did not affect the amount of damage to the DNA, as detected by the levels of γH2A.X at the sites of damage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Overexpression of H2A(K119/120R) reduces H2A.Z loading at DSBs compared to control cells and cells overexpressing wild-type H2A.
source: We observed a reduction in H2A.Z loading at DSBs in cells overexpressing H2A(K119/120R) compared to control cells and cells overexpressing wild-type H2A (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by qChIP data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The FRRUC-dependent mono-ubiquitylation of H2A is required for proper H2A.Z loading.
source: This result is in agreement with the fact that only wild-type RNF68, but not the two inactive RNF68 mutants, rescued the defect of H2A.Z loading (Figure 6E), and indicates that the FRRUC-dependent mono-ubiquitylation of H2A is required for proper H2A.Z loading.
evidence: Based on integration of H2A mutant and RNF68 mutant rescue experiments.

claim: H2A mono-ubiquitylation is not impaired upon H2A.Z silencing.
source: While H2A mono-ubiquitylation was not impaired upon H2A.Z silencing (Figure 7A), we detected significantly more nascent RNA transcript production near DSB sites in H2A.Z depleted cells compared control cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Significantly more nascent RNA transcript production occurs near DSB sites in H2A.Z depleted cells compared to control cells.
source: While H2A mono-ubiquitylation was not impaired upon H2A.Z silencing (Figure 7A), we detected significantly more nascent RNA transcript production near DSB sites in H2A.Z depleted cells compared control cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by YFP-MS2 reporter assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: H2A.Z silencing does not have a negative effect on FokI nuclease levels.
source: [H2A.Z silencing did not have a negative effect on FokI nuclease levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)].
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a decrease in both 5-EU incorporation and phosphorylation of RNAPII on Ser2 at laser induced damage sites in control cells, and this decrease is significantly less in H2A.Z depleted cells.
source: Similarly, there was a decrease in both 5-EU incorporation and phosphorylation of RNAPII on Ser2 at laser induced damage sites in control cells, and this decrease was significantly less in cells in which H2A.Z was depleted (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: Supported by 5-EU incorporation and RNAPII Ser2 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: H2A.Z depletion induces a reduction in the phosphorylation of RPA2 on Ser4, Ser8, and Ser33 as well as in the phosphorylation of CHK1 (Ser317).
source: Similar to the depletion of the FRRUC, H2A.Z depletion in both U-2OS and MIA-PaCa-2 cells also induced a reduction in the phosphorylation of RPA2 on Ser4, Ser8, and Ser33 as well as in the phosphorylation of CHK1 (Ser317) (Figure 7E), all events necessary for efficient HRR repair.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: No changes in γH2A.X levels are observed upon H2A.Z silencing.
source: Again, we observed no changes in γH2A.X levels upon H2A.Z silencing, showing that the amount of DNA damage induction was similar in all conditions (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: H2A.Z is required for efficient HRR.
source: Finally, we found that H2A.Z is required for efficient HRR (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by DR-GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: H2A.Z incorporation contributes to transcriptional silencing after DNA damage, as well as efficient DNA damage signaling and HRR.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that H2A.Z incorporation, which is downstream to the FRRUC and H2AK119Ub1, contributes to transcriptional silencing after DNA damage, as well as efficient DNA damage signaling and HRR.
evidence: Based on integration of multiple H2A.Z depletion experiments.

claim: The FRRUC is recruited to sites of DNA damage in a PARP1- and TIMELESS-dependent manner.
source: We show here that the FRRUC is recruited to sites of DNA damage in a PARP1- and TIMELESS-dependent manner.
evidence: Based on integration of recruitment experiments with PARP1 and TIMELESS depletion/inhibition.

claim: The FRRUC is required for efficient mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119 at DNA damage sites.
source: Our results demonstrate that the complex is required for efficient mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119, a decrease of H2A levels at DSBs, localization of the histone variant H2A.Z to sites of DNA damage, transcriptional repression, DSB signaling, and proper HRR (see model in Figure 7F).
evidence: Based on integration of multiple experimental results.

claim: The FRRUC promotes a decrease of H2A levels at DSBs.
source: Our results demonstrate that the complex is required for efficient mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119, a decrease of H2A levels at DSBs, localization of the histone variant H2A.Z to sites of DNA damage, transcriptional repression, DSB signaling, and proper HRR (see model in Figure 7F).
evidence: Based on qChIP data showing H2A reduction is FRRUC-dependent.

claim: The FRRUC promotes localization of H2A.Z to sites of DNA damage.
source: Our results demonstrate that the complex is required for efficient mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119, a decrease of H2A levels at DSBs, localization of the histone variant H2A.Z to sites of DNA damage, transcriptional repression, DSB signaling, and proper HRR (see model in Figure 7F).
evidence: Based on qChIP and dSTORM data showing H2A.Z recruitment is FRRUC-dependent.

claim: The FRRUC promotes transcriptional repression at DNA damage sites.
source: Our results demonstrate that the complex is required for efficient mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119, a decrease of H2A levels at DSBs, localization of the histone variant H2A.Z to sites of DNA damage, transcriptional repression, DSB signaling, and proper HRR (see model in Figure 7F).
evidence: Based on multiple transcription reporter assays.

claim: The FRRUC promotes DSB signaling.
source: Our results demonstrate that the complex is required for efficient mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119, a decrease of H2A levels at DSBs, localization of the histone variant H2A.Z to sites of DNA damage, transcriptional repression, DSB signaling, and proper HRR (see model in Figure 7F).
evidence: Based on DDR marker experiments showing reduced signaling upon FRRUC depletion.

claim: The FRRUC promotes proper HRR.
source: Our results demonstrate that the complex is required for efficient mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119, a decrease of H2A levels at DSBs, localization of the histone variant H2A.Z to sites of DNA damage, transcriptional repression, DSB signaling, and proper HRR (see model in Figure 7F).
evidence: Based on DR-GFP reporter assay data.

claim: Transcriptional silencing in response to genotoxic stress facilitates DNA damage resolution by ensuring that the transcriptional machinery does not interfere sterically with DNA damage repair factors.
source: In response to genotoxic stress, transcriptional silencing is thought to facilitate DNA damage resolution by ensuring that the transcriptional machinery does not interfere sterically with DNA damage repair factors (e.g. by avoiding the collision of the elongating RNA Polymerase complex with DNA repair complexes) (Uckelmann and Sixma, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Uckelmann and Sixma, 2017.

claim: Several factors and complexes have been implicated in DNA damage-induced transcriptional repression.
source: Several factors and complexes, such as NurRD, PBAF, ENL, RNF8, NELF-E, and RNF51-UBR5 have been implicated in the DNA damage-induced transcriptional repression (Awwad et al., 2017; Chou et al., 2010; Gong et al., 2017; Kakarougkas et al., 2014; Paul and Wang, 2017; Sanchez et al., 2016, 2010; Ui et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119 is largely impaired by the depletion of the FRRUC.
source: We found that the mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119 is largely impaired by the depletion of the FRRUC.
evidence: Based on immunofluorescence and qChIP data.

claim: The FRRUC is a major contributor to the mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119 in transcriptional regulation.
source: Similarly, the FRRUC is a major contributor to the mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119 in transcriptional regulation (Blackledge et al., 2014; Rose et al., 2016; Taherbhoy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Blackledge et al., 2014; Rose et al., 2016; Taherbhoy et al., 2015.

claim: The FRRUC is necessary for the proper recruitment of RNF51-RNF2 and RNF110-RNF2 in response to genotoxic stress.
source: Our results show that the FRRUC is necessary for the proper recruitment of these two cPRC1s in response to genotoxic stress.
evidence: Based on live cell imaging recruitment experiments.

claim: The FRRUC is the most upstream ubiquitin ligase in charge of mono-ubiquitylating histone H2A on K119 at DNA damage sites.
source: Moreover, our findings suggest that the FRRUC is the most upstream ubiquitin ligase in charge of mono-ubiquitylating histone H2A on K119 and that, subsequently, cPRC1s maintain this modification.
evidence: Based on integration of recruitment kinetics and dependency experiments.

claim: Compared to the recruitment of 70 DNA repair proteins measured in a recent study, FBXL10, RNF68, and RNF2 display very fast recruitment.
source: Interestingly, a recent study measured the kinetics of recruitment of 70 DNA repair proteins to laser-induced DNA damage sites in HeLa cells (Aleksandrov et al., 2018). Compared to the recruitment of these 70 proteins, FBXL10, RNF68, and RNF2 display a very fast recruitment, suggesting that this represent one of the most upstream events in response to genotoxic stress.
evidence: Based on comparison to published kinetics data from Aleksandrov et al., 2018.

claim: The DNA damage response frequently re-purposes the function of specific transcriptional regulators to enact DNA repair.
source: The DNA damage response frequently re-purposes the function of specific transcriptional regulators to enact DNA repair (Sarcinella et al., 2007; Shiloh and Ziv, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sarcinella et al., 2007; Shiloh and Ziv, 2013.

claim: The presence, localization, and activity of the FRRUC is required for an efficient H2A/H2A.Z exchange at DNA lesions.
source: Our results reveal that the presence, localization, and activity of the FRRUC, in addition to mono-ubiquitylate H2A on K119 (as in unstressed cells), is also required for an efficient H2A/H2A.Z exchange at DNA lesions.
evidence: Based on integration of H2A and H2A.Z qChIP and imaging data.

claim: H2A.Z is not required for H2A mono-ubiquitylation.
source: Notably, whereas H2A.Z is not required for H2A mono-ubiquitylation, the FRRUC-dependent mono-ubiquitylation of H2A is required for proper H2A.Z loading.
evidence: Based on H2A.Z depletion experiments showing no effect on H2AK119Ub1.

claim: The FRRUC-dependent mono-ubiquitylation of H2A is required for proper H2A.Z loading.
source: Notably, whereas H2A.Z is not required for H2A mono-ubiquitylation, the FRRUC-dependent mono-ubiquitylation of H2A is required for proper H2A.Z loading.
evidence: Based on H2A mutant and FRRUC depletion experiments.

claim: H2A.Z has been shown to function in the early stages of DNA repair.
source: H2A.Z has been shown to function in the early stages of DNA repair (Adkins et al., 2013; Alatwi and Downs, 2015; Gursoy-Yuzugullu et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2015; Kalocsay et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: H2A.Z is rapidly, yet transiently, recruited to DSBs.
source: H2A.Z is rapidly, yet transiently, recruited to DSBs (Alatwi and Downs, 2015; Gursoy-Yuzugullu et al., 2015; Kalocsay et al., 2009; Kusch et al., 2004; Nishibuchi et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: H2A.Z shares 56% sequence identity with H2A.
source: H2A.Z shares 56% sequence identity with H2A and the differences account for a structurally less stable interface between H2A.Z and the H3-H4 subunits of the nucleosome.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of histone variant sequences.

claim: H2A.Z makes weakened, loose nucleosomes that are easy to bend and disassemble, leading to a more accessible chromatin.
source: In fact, H2A.Z appears to make weakened, loose nucleosomes that are easy to bend and disassemble, leading to a more accessible chromatin (Bönisch et al., 2012; Jin and Felsenfeld, 2007; Jin et al., 2009; Suto et al., 2000; Xu et al., 2012), which may favor recruitment of DNA repair factors.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bönisch et al., 2012; Jin and Felsenfeld, 2007; Jin et al., 2009; Suto et al., 2000; Xu et al., 2012.

claim: H2A.Z has been associated with both positive and negative transcriptional regulation depending on its post-translational modifications.
source: H2A.Z has been associated with both positive and negative transcriptional regulation depending on its post-translational modifications (Guillemette and Gaudreau, 2006; Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guillemette and Gaudreau, 2006; Hu et al., 2013.

claim: Mono-ubiquitylation of H2A.Z on K120 and K121 is correlated with transcriptional silencing.
source: Mono-ubiquitylation of H2A.Z on K120 and K121 is correlated with transcriptional silencing (Draker et al., 2011; Sarcinella et al., 2007), whereas H2A.Z acetylation on its N-terminus is associated with transcriptional activity (Valdés-Mora et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Draker et al., 2011; Sarcinella et al., 2007.

claim: H2A.Z acetylation on its N-terminus is associated with transcriptional activity.
source: Mono-ubiquitylation of H2A.Z on K120 and K121 is correlated with transcriptional silencing (Draker et al., 2011; Sarcinella et al., 2007), whereas H2A.Z acetylation on its N-terminus is associated with transcriptional activity (Valdés-Mora et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Valdés-Mora et al., 2012.

claim: Mono-ubiquitylation of H2A.Z has been attributed to RNF2 activity.
source: Interestingly, mono-ubiquitylation of H2A.Z has been attributed to RNF2 activity (Sarcinella et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sarcinella et al., 2007.

claim: The FRRUC could be involved in transcriptional silencing by mono-ubiquitylating H2A, facilitating exchange of H2A with H2A.Z, and mono-ubiquitylating H2A.Z.
source: Thus, the FRRUC could be involved in transcriptional silencing by several non-exclusive – and, perhaps, linked – means: (i) mono-ubiquitylating H2A, (ii) facilitating exchange of a subpopulation of H2A with H2A.Z, and (iii), mono-ubiquitylating H2A.Z.
evidence: Based on integration of experimental results and speculation about mechanisms.

claim: Upon DNA damage, H2A.Z can simultaneously 'loosen' the chromatin to facilitate access to DNA repair factors and mediate transcriptional silencing.
source: It is possible that, upon DNA damage, H2A.Z can simultaneously 'loosen' the chromatin to facilitate the access to DNA repair factors (this is the reason for which a subpopulation of H2A is exchanged for H2A.Z) and mediate transcriptional silencing (conceivably, by its mono-ubiquitylation).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental results.

claim: PARP1 has been implicated in H2A displacement and chromatin decondensation after DNA damage.
source: Accordingly, PARP1 has been implicated in H2A displacement and chromatin decondensation after DNA damage (Sellou et al., 2016; Strickfaden et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sellou et al., 2016; Strickfaden et al., 2016.

claim: The regulation of FBXL10, RNF68, and RNF2 by TIMELESS is unusual since the recruitment of other PARP-dependent factors is not affected by TIMELESS depletion.
source: The regulation of FBXL10, RNF68, and RNF2 by TIMELESS is unusual since the recruitment of other factors downstream of PARP, such as XRCC1 and Ligase 3 (that are required for single strand break and base excision repair), is affected by PARP1 silencing (Campalans et al., 2013; Godon et al., 2008; Mortusewicz et al., 2006; Okano et al., 2003), but not by TIMELESS depletion, suggesting a specific role of TIMELESS in controlling DSB repair.
evidence: Based on comparison of TIMELESS effects on different DNA repair factors and citations.

claim: In response to DNA damage, H2A and H2A.X are ubiquitylated on both K13 and K15 in addition to mono-ubiquitylation of K119/K120.
source: In response to DNA damage, in addition to the mono-ubiquitylation of K119/K120, H2A and H2A.X are also ubiquitylated on both K13 and K15.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of histone ubiquitylation in DDR.

claim: RNF8 decorates H1 type linker histones and L3MBTL2 with K63-linked ubiquitin chains in response to DNA damage.
source: This event requires two steps: first, an RNF ubiquitin ligase, namely RNF8, decorates H1 type linker histones and L3MBTL2 with K63-linked ubiquitin chains (Mandemaker et al., 2017; Nowsheen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mandemaker et al., 2017; Nowsheen et al., 2018.

claim: RNF168 recognizes K63-linked ubiquitin chains on H1 and L3MBTL2 and mono-ubiquitylates H2A and H2A.X on K13 and K15.
source: Next, these chains are recognized by RNF168, another RNF ubiquitin ligase, that mono-ubiquitylates H2A and H2A.X on K13 and K15 (Gatti et al., 2012; Leung et al., 2014; Mattiroli et al., 2012; Thorslund et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gatti et al., 2012; Leung et al., 2014; Mattiroli et al., 2012; Thorslund et al., 2015.

claim: A K63 chain is built on mono-ubiquitylated H2A and H2A.X, although the ubiquitin ligase involved in this elongation step is still debated.
source: Ultimately, a K63 chain (and, possibly other kind of ubiquitin chains) is/are built on mono-ubiquitylated H2A and H2A.X, although the ubiquitin ligase involved in this elongation step is still debated (Uckelmann and Sixma, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Uckelmann and Sixma, 2017.

claim: Ubiquitin chains on H2A and H2A.X are crucial for the recruitment of DNA repair factors necessary for both efficient HRR and NHEJ.
source: These ubiquitin chains are crucial for the recruitment of DNA repair factors, an event necessary for both efficient HRR and NHEJ (Schwertman et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schwertman et al., 2016.

claim: Neither RNF8 nor RNF168 can ubiquitylate K119 and K120 of H2A/H2A.X.
source: Notably, neither RNF8 nor RNF168 can ubiquitylate K119 and K120 of H2A/H2A.X, and, vice versa, RNF2 and its interacting PCGFs are unable to ubiquitylate K13 and K15 (Mattiroli et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mattiroli et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2004.

claim: RNF2 and its interacting PCGFs are unable to ubiquitylate K13 and K15 of H2A/H2A.X.
source: Notably, neither RNF8 nor RNF168 can ubiquitylate K119 and K120 of H2A/H2A.X, and, vice versa, RNF2 and its interacting PCGFs are unable to ubiquitylate K13 and K15 (Mattiroli et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mattiroli et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2004.

claim: The ubiquitylation of K119 and K120 in H2A/H2A.X is involved in the recruitment of DNA repair factors.
source: Our findings show that, similar to the ubiquitylation of K13 and K15, the ubiquitylation of K119 and K120 in H2A/H2A.X is also involved in the recruitment of DNA repair factors.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing reduced DNA repair factor recruitment upon FRRUC depletion.

claim: ATM inhibition increases the recruitment of the FRRUC.
source: Intriguingly, while the FRRUC is necessary for an efficient DDR, ATM inhibition increases the recruitment of the FRRUC.
evidence: Based on observed recruitment kinetics with ATM inhibitor.

claim: ATM might limit the spread of the FRRUC and subsequent H2A mono-ubiquitylation to maintain the signal at DSB proximities.
source: ATM might limit the spread of the FRRUC and the subsequent H2A mono-ubiquitylation to maintain the signal at DSB proximities.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of ATM inhibition effects on FRRUC recruitment.

claim: The recruitment of the FRRUC represents an early and critical regulatory step in HRR.
source: We propose that the recruitment of the FRRUC represents an early and critical regulatory step in HRR.
evidence: Based on integration of all experimental results showing early recruitment and requirement for HRR.
